opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one I think about a lot. The first thing I'd say is that law, in the broad sense, is a really hard target. Legal language is deliberately ambiguous in places. Phrases like "reasonable" or "in good faith" exist precisely because the drafters wanted humans, judges and juries, to fill in the meaning based on context. So if your goal is to take, say, the entire tax code or contract law and turn it into a set of logical axioms that you then reason about mechanically, I think you're going to struggle. That's not where the leverage is.

But there's a huge space of rules that look like law and behave much more like specifications. Think about access control policies in the cloud, network configuration rules, compliance requirements like "data from this region must never leave this region," or "only these principals can decrypt this key." Those are policies that organizations write down and want to be true, and they're often precise enough, or can be made precise enough, that you can formalize them. And once you've formalized them, you can ask questions like "is there any possible request that would allow access to this bucket from outside my organization?" and get a proof that the answer is no, or a concrete counterexample. That's where automated reasoning really shines. It's not about one test case. It's about all possible cases.

What I've found is that the act of formalizing is valuable in itself, even when it's hard. When you sit down with people and try to pin down what a policy actually means, you discover that different stakeholders have different interpretations. The lawyers think it means one thing, the engineers implemented another, and the customer assumed a third. Formalization surfaces those disagreements. So part of the value isn't just the proof at the end; it's the conversation that the formalization forces.

The other thing that's changed the picture recently is generative AI. Large language models are pretty good at taking natural language, a policy document, a regulation, a set of HR rules, and producing a candidate formalization. They're not perfect, and you can't just trust them, but now the workflow can be: the model proposes a logical translation, a human domain expert reviews it, and the automated reasoning tools check consistency, find contradictions, and later verify whether a given answer or action complies. Automated reasoning becomes a check on the LLM rather than requiring humans to do all the painful translation work up front. That's a big part of why I think we're going to see these techniques reach far more people.

So my answer is: be pragmatic. Pick domains where the rules matter, where mistakes are expensive, and where the meaning can be pinned down with reasonable effort. Leave the parts that are intentionally open-textured to humans. And use the tools to make explicit where the ambiguity is, because knowing exactly where the gray areas are is itself enormously useful.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you mean by "law," and the trick is to find the places where there's actually a well-defined question hiding inside the messy human stuff.

So take something like tax law. There are enormous pieces of the tax code that are, frankly, just arithmetic with branching. If your income is above this threshold, and you filed jointly, and this deduction applies, then this is the number. That's a program. It's a badly written program, written in English by committees over decades, but it's a program. And for that kind of thing, automated reasoning is a fantastic fit, because you can encode the rules, you can ask whether two interpretations are consistent, you can find the corner cases where the rules contradict each other, and you can prove that a piece of software that implements the rules actually does what the rules say.

Where it gets hard is the parts of law that are intentionally vague. "Reasonable care." "Good faith." Those terms exist precisely because the drafters didn't want to pin them down; they wanted a judge or a jury to apply judgment later. And you can't formalize judgment that nobody's made yet. I don't think we should try. If you force a definition of "reasonable" into a logic, you've just invented a new law that nobody voted for.

So the way I think about it at Amazon, and in the work we've done on things like access control policies and compliance, is: don't try to formalize the whole thing. Formalize the parts that have a precise meaning, be explicit about the boundary, and then let the human reason about the vague parts with the tool giving them certainty about everything else. So an auditor might come in and say, "Is it possible for anyone outside this organization to read this bucket?" That's a crisp question, and we can answer it with a proof. Whether the organization should have been storing that data in the first place is a different kind of question, and we leave that to the humans.

And actually, I'd say the biggest value often isn't in the answer, it's in the formalization itself. When you sit down with a lawyer or a policy person and try to write the rule precisely, you discover that the rule was ambiguous, or that two people in the room had different readings of it. The tool forces the conversation. So even in cases where you never run a solver, the act of trying to make it precise is worth something.

The other thing I'd flag is that the technology has shifted the economics here. Ten years ago, the cost of writing the formal model was the bottleneck, so you only did it for very high-value things. Now with large language models you can get a first draft of a formalization from natural language, and then use the solver to check it, and use the solver's counterexamples to go back and refine. That loop makes it practical to tackle a lot more of the "boring but important" regulatory text than we could before. It doesn't solve the vagueness problem, but it makes the crisp parts much cheaper to get right.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between deciding what the rules should mean and checking the consequences of rules once you’ve made them precise. Law has ambiguity, and sometimes that ambiguity is intentional. Automated reasoning doesn’t make that go away.

But there are narrower questions where it can be very useful. Suppose you have a policy that says who can access a particular piece of data. You can ask, “Is there any way someone outside this group could get access?” That’s a precise question, and reasoning can help you answer it across all the possibilities, rather than just the examples you happened to test.

The qualification is that you’ve proved something about the model you wrote down. You still need people to judge whether that model captures the intended policy. So I think of this as a collaboration: people supply the interpretation and intent, and the tools help uncover consequences, contradictions, and cases that people might otherwise miss.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between deciding what the law ought to mean and checking whether a system behaves according to a particular interpretation. We’re not trying to automate the judge. There are questions of intent and context where people have to make a judgment. But once you’ve made that judgment, there can be a tremendous amount of reasoning needed to understand its consequences.

Take access control: you might have a policy that says certain people can see certain data, except under these conditions. Even if each individual rule is simple, their interactions can be very difficult to understand. Automated reasoning can help answer, “Is there any way someone outside this group could get access?” And if there is, it can give you an example.

Of course, you still have to ask whether the formal policy captures what you intended. A proof doesn’t remove that responsibility. But it lets you separate that question from whether the implementation actually follows the policy, and that’s a very useful separation.
